The Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation, a cornerstone of classical mechanics, is generalized in this work to apply to systems containing fractional derivatives. This extension builds upon and broadens the foundational work of Rabei et al., adapting their approach to accommodate the more general framework of fractional-order dynamics. By incorporating fractional derivatives into the formulation, the resulting theory becomes capable of describing a wider class of physical systems, including those exhibiting nonconservative or memory-dependent behavior.

Central to this development is the derivation of the Hamilton-Jacobi function in configuration space. This is accomplished using methods that are analogous to those employed in conventional mechanics, thereby preserving the structural elegance and interpretive clarity of the classical formalism. The parallel construction ensures that familiar techniques and physical intuitions carry over naturally into the fractional setting, while the underlying equations are suitably modified to account for the fractional derivative operators.

To demonstrate the practical utility of this formalism, two specific problems are examined in detail. These illustrative examples serve to clarify the procedure and to show how the generalized Hamilton-Jacobi equation can be applied to concrete physical situations. # Generalization of the Hamilton-Jacobi Formulation to Fractional Systems

## Introduction

The study of fractional calculus has attracted considerable attention in recent decades due to its capacity to describe physical systems characterized by nonconservative forces, memory effects, and dissipation. Classical mechanics, formulated through the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian approaches, provides an elegant description of conservative systems. However, many real-world phenomena involve nonconservative interactions that resist description within the traditional framework. To address this limitation, fractional derivatives have been incorporated into the formulations of mechanics, allowing for a more comprehensive treatment of these systems.

Building on the prior work of Rabei et al., this study generalizes the Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation to accommodate systems containing fractional derivatives. The Hamilton-Jacobi theory, a cornerstone of classical mechanics, offers a powerful method for solving dynamical problems by transforming them into the problem of finding a suitable generating function. Extending this formalism to the fractional domain enables its application to a broader class of physical systems.

## Theoretical Framework

In conventional mechanics, the Hamilton-Jacobi equation is derived through a canonical transformation that reduces the transformed Hamiltonian to zero, yielding the principal function known as Hamilton's principal function. This function is defined in configuration space and serves as the generator of the motion, encoding the complete dynamical evolution of the system.

Following an analogous procedure, we construct the Hamilton-Jacobi function for fractional systems within configuration space. Beginning with the fractional Lagrangian formulation and the corresponding fractional canonical momenta, the fractional Hamiltonian is established. The canonical transformation that renders the new Hamiltonian identically zero then leads directly to the fractional Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation. In this manner, the Hamilton-Jacobi function is obtained in a form that parallels the conventional treatment, with fractional derivatives replacing their integer-order counterparts where appropriate.

The resulting equation governs the evolution of the principal function and, once solved, provides the complete solution to the equations of motion for the fractional system. This approach preserves the structural elegance of classical Hamilton-Jacobi theory while accommodating the additional complexity introduced by fractional-order derivatives.

## Illustrative Applications

To demonstrate the validity and utility of the proposed formalism, two representative problems are examined. In each case, the fractional Hamilton-Jacobi equation is constructed and solved to determine the equations of motion. The solutions obtained through this method are then compared with those derived using Agrawal's formalism, a well-established framework for treating fractional variational problems.

The comparison reveals that the results produced by the generalized Hamilton-Jacobi approach are in exact agreement with those obtained from Agrawal's formalism. This concordance confirms the consistency and reliability of the proposed method, establishing it as a legitimate alternative for analyzing systems governed by fractional derivatives.

## Conclusion

By extending the Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation to the fractional domain, this work broadens the applicability of a fundamental technique of classical mechanics. The successful validation through two demonstrative examples, which yield results identical to those of Agrawal's formalism, confirms that the formalism is both correct and practically applicable to fractional systems. This generalization contributes to the ongoing development of fractional mechanics and offers a valuable tool for the investigation of nonconservative and dissipative physical systems.

# The Hamilton-Jacobi Approach and Rabei's Contributions

## Introduction

The Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) formulation represents one of the most elegant and powerful frameworks in classical mechanics and theoretical physics. Building upon the foundational work of William Rowan Hamilton and Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, this approach has been significantly extended and applied to modern problems through the contributions of researchers such as Eqab M. Rabei, whose work has advanced our understanding of constrained systems and fractional dynamics.

## The Classical Hamilton-Jacobi Theory

The Hamilton-Jacobi equation emerges as a reformulation of classical mechanics that unifies the study of mechanics, optics, and wave phenomena. At its core, the theory seeks a canonical transformation that reduces the problem of solving the equations of motion to finding a single function—Hamilton's principal function, often denoted as *S*.

The fundamental Hamilton-Jacobi equation takes the form:

$$H\left(q_i, \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_i}, t\right) + \frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = 0$$

where *H* is the Hamiltonian of the system, *q_i* represents the generalized coordinates, and *S* is the action functional. This partial differential equation provides a bridge between classical and quantum mechanics, particularly through its connection to the eikonal approximation and the Schrödinger equation.

## Rabei's Extensions to Constrained Systems

Eqab M. Rabei has made notable contributions by extending the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism to handle **constrained systems** and singular Lagrangians. Traditional approaches to constrained dynamics, such as Dirac's method, involve the classification of constraints into first-class and second-class categories. Rabei and collaborators developed an alternative treatment based on the Hamilton-Jacobi approach.

In this framework, constrained systems are treated by considering the equations of motion as total differential equations in many variables. The integrability conditions of these equations naturally reproduce the constraints, offering a more systematic and often simpler pathway compared to conventional methods.

## Applications to Fractional Calculus

A particularly innovative direction in Rabei's research involves the application of the Hamilton-Jacobi formulation to **fractional-order systems**. Fractional calculus, which generalizes differentiation and integration to non-integer orders, has become increasingly important in describing systems with memory effects, dissipation, and complex dynamics.

Rabei's work on fractional Hamilton-Jacobi theory extends the classical formalism to accommodate systems governed by fractional derivatives. This has opened new avenues for modeling nonconservative and dissipative systems, which were traditionally difficult to treat within standard Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics.

## Significance and Impact

The synthesis of Hamilton and Jacobi's classical work with modern extensions by researchers like Rabei demonstrates the enduring relevance of this theoretical framework. The Hamilton-Jacobi approach continues to serve as:

- A fundamental tool in **theoretical physics** and celestial mechanics
- A bridge connecting **classical and quantum theories**
- A practical method for analyzing **constrained and singular systems**
- A foundation for exploring **fractional and nonconservative dynamics**

## Conclusion

The evolution of Hamilton-Jacobi theory—from its nineteenth-century origins to its contemporary applications in constrained and fractional systems—illustrates the dynamic nature of mathematical physics. Rabei's contributions have helped keep this classical framework at the forefront of modern research, providing physicists and mathematicians with versatile tools for tackling increasingly complex problems in dynamics and field theory.

The Hamilton-Jacobi formalism provides a powerful framework for analyzing constrained and unconstrained dynamical systems, offering an alternative to conventional Lagrangian and Hamiltonian approaches. In this paper, we extend the Hamilton-Jacobi treatment to fractional dynamical systems, wherein the classical derivatives are replaced by fractional derivatives in the sense of the Riemann-Liouville and Caputo definitions. Beginning from a fractional Lagrangian, we systematically construct the corresponding fractional Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation and derive the associated equations of motion. The results indicate that the Hamilton-Jacobi approach constitutes an effective and systematic tool for investigating fractional-order systems, with potential applications in the modeling of dissipative processes, non-conservative forces, and complex physical phenomena characterized by memory and nonlocal effects.

# Fractional Hamilton-Jacobi Formulation for Systems with Fractional Derivatives

## Abstract

We present a generalization of the Hamilton-Jacobi partial differential equation to dynamical systems governed by fractional-order derivatives, wherein classical integer-order kinematics are replaced by Riemann-Liouville and Caputo fractional operators. Beginning from the fractional Lagrangian formulation, we construct the corresponding fractional Hamiltonian through a generalized Legendre transformation that accounts for the non-local character of fractional differentiation. Introducing canonical momenta conjugate to both left and right fractional derivatives of the generalized coordinates, we derive the fractional Hamilton-Jacobi equation as a first-order partial differential equation for Hamilton's principal function $S$ defined over configuration space.

The resulting formalism yields a fractional analogue of the classical relation

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} + H\!\left(q,\, {}_aD_t^{\alpha} q,\, \frac{\partial S}{\partial q},\, t\right) = 0,
$$

in which the memory-dependent structure of the system enters explicitly through the fractional derivative terms. We demonstrate that the fractional canonical equations of motion are recovered as characteristics of this partial differential equation, and that in the limit $\alpha \rightarrow 1$ the standard Hamilton-Jacobi theory is fully restored. The construction of the Hamilton-Jacobi function $S$ in configuration space permits separation of variables for suitable systems and provides a systematic route to constants of motion and complete integrals for fractional dynamical models. Illustrative examples confirm consistency with the fractional Euler-Lagrange and Hamiltonian equations, establishing the fractional Hamilton-Jacobi equation as a coherent generalization suitable for describing non-conservative and non-local physical systems.

---

*Keywords:* fractional derivatives, Hamilton-Jacobi equation, fractional Hamiltonian mechanics, Riemann-Liouville operators, non-conservative systems
